procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated September 21, 1970 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in A.S. No. 476 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Devendra Doss appealed against the Subordinate Judge's judgment to the High Court. The High Court found that Narayan Doss was not a North-Indian Brahmin and therefore not entitled to being considered as a possible successor to the office of the mohunt. The High Court further held that since Devendra Doss was the senior disciple of Chetandoss he should by the rule of custom succeed to the office of the mohunt upon the death of Chetandoss. On these grounds the High Court upheld the plaintiff's appeal and gave a declaration in his favour and also an injunction against Narayan Doss from interfering with the affairs of the Mutt.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Rajendra Ram Doss appealed to the Supreme Court with certificates from the High Court's decision.

decision.appeal_result: In the view that we take of this matter the appeal fails and is dismissed.
directions: In the peculiar circumstances of this case we make no orders to costs.
All the stay orders passed in this matter by this Court shall stand vacated.

issue.issue_text: Whether a party can rely on the doctrine of estoppel arising from a recital in a deed, if that party, instead of relying on the estoppel at trial, joins issue on the fact in question.

facts: A deed (Ex. B-1) contained a recital stating that the defendant, Rajendra Ram Doss, was a North-Indian Brahmin.
This recital could have formed the basis for a plea of estoppel against the plaintiff.
However, at trial, the defendant did not rely on this plea of estoppel.
Instead, the defendant "joined issue" with the plaintiff on the factual question of whether he was a North-Indian Brahmin.
An issue was specifically raised on this question, and both parties adduced evidence.
law: The Court cited the principle from the case of *Young and Anr. v. Raincock*.
This principle states that if a party who is entitled to the benefit of an estoppel, instead of relying on it, "goes to issue on the fact," they put the matter "at large."
When a matter is put "at large," the court is free to decide the factual question based on the evidence and may disregard the estoppel.
application: The defendant, Rajendra Ram Doss, had the opportunity to rely on the estoppel arising from the recital in the deed.
By failing to do so and instead actively contesting the factual question of his Brahmin status, he waived his right to the estoppel.
His actions opened the entire matter for the trial court to decide based on the evidence presented by both sides, rather than being bound by the statement in the deed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that because the defendant chose to join issue on the factual question of his Brahmin status instead of relying on the estoppel from the deed's recital, he could not later use the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the plaintiff from proving the contrary. The defendant's actions put the matter "at large," allowing the court to decide the issue based on the evidence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant, who was found not to be a North-Indian Brahmin, could be appointed as the mohunt when the customary rule required the successor to be a North-Indian Brahmin.

facts: Succession to the office of Mohunt is regulated by a custom which has two conditions: the successor must be the senior disciple of the last reigning mohunt, and the successor must be a North-Indian Brahmin.
The appellant, Rajendra Ram Doss, claimed the office.
The High Court found as a matter of fact that the appellant was not a North-Indian Brahmin, a finding the Supreme Court accepted.
law: The customary rule for succession to the office of Mohunt requires the successor to satisfy two conditions: being the senior-most disciple and being a North-Indian Brahmin.
The requirement of being a North-Indian Brahmin is an "equally customary rule" and is essential for eligibility.
application: The Supreme Court applied the established facts directly to the customary rule.
It noted that even assuming the appellant satisfied the first condition of being the senior-most disciple of a former mohunt, he failed to meet the second, equally important condition.
The Court stated that it was "not possible to make Rajendra Ram Doss the Mohunt for the simple reason that he has been found not to be a North-Indian Brahmin."
The failure to meet the mandatory requirement of being a North-Indian Brahmin was a complete disqualification for the office.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, deciding that he could not be appointed as the mohunt because he failed to satisfy the essential and mandatory customary rule that the successor must be a North-Indian Brahmin. This disqualification stood even if he met the other part of the custom regarding discipleship.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a party can rely on the doctrine of estoppel arising from a recital in a deed, if that party, instead of relying on the estoppel at trial, joins issue on the fact in question.
appellant_arguments: The respondent (Devendra Doss) is bound by the agreement (Ex. B-1) which explicitly states that the appellant (Rajendra Ram Doss) is a North-Indian Brahmin.
Since the respondent claims through Chetandoss, who was a party to the agreement, he is estopped from denying the facts recited in it.
respondent_arguments: The appellant waived the right to rely on estoppel by failing to invoke the plea before the trial court.

The appellant, instead of relying on estoppel, joined issue with the respondent on the factual question of whether he was a North-Indian Brahmin, and evidence was adduced by both sides, putting the matter at large for the court to decide.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant, who was found not to be a North-Indian Brahmin, could be appointed as the mohunt when the customary rule required the successor to be a North-Indian Brahmin.
appellant_arguments: The period of the previous mohunt (Chetandoss) was a departure from custom and should be treated as an 'interregnum' and ignored.
Succession should revert to the line of the mohunt before that (Narayandass).
As the senior disciple of Narayandass, the appellant is the rightful successor once the interregnum is disregarded.
respondent_arguments: The appellant is not a North-Indian Brahmin, a necessary qualification for the office of mohunt, and is therefore not entitled to be a successor.
The respondent, as the senior disciple of the last reigning mohunt (Chetandoss), is the rightful successor according to the established rule of custom.

cases.principle: If a party who is entitled to rely on estoppel instead joins issue on the fact, he puts the matter at large and can no longer rely on the estoppel.

cases.case_name: Greer v. Kettle Re Parent Trust & Finance Co. Ltd.
cases.principle: To confirm the principle that a party who fails to invoke the doctrine of estoppel and instead joins issue on the facts cannot later rely on it.

cases.case_name: Annasami Pillai and Ors. v. Ramakrishna Mudaliar and Anr.
cases.principle: When there is a break in a customary rule, any correction must be in the direction of re-establishing the rule of custom.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A party who is entitled to rely on an estoppel arising from a recital in a deed waives that right if, instead of pleading the estoppel, they join issue on the fact in question, thereby putting the matter at large for the court to decide based on evidence. In matters of succession governed by custom, where a break in the customary line has occurred, any correction must be directed toward re-establishing the rule of custom.
obiter: Where a person who had no right to the office of a trustee according to the established rule of devolution acquires a title by prescription, but restores it to one who could have taken the office according to the rules, such a transfer may be treated as an exception to the general doctrine that a trusteeship is not assignable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant cannot be appointed as the mohunt for the simple reason that he was found not to be a North-Indian Brahmin, a necessary qualification under the rule of custom. As the appellant is unqualified, his proposal to ignore the previous mohunt's tenure and revert to the prior line of succession would break the custom beyond repair. Therefore, the only way to save and re-establish the custom is to appoint the respondent, who is qualified and is the senior-most disciple of the last reigning mohunt.
legal_tests_applied: If a party who is entitled to take advantage of an estoppel instead of relying on it goes to issue on the fact, he puts the matter at large, and the court may disregard the estoppel.
The rule of custom should prevail in all cases and if any aberrations have to be corrected such correction must take us in the direction of re-establishing the rule of custom.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant waived his right to rely on the doctrine of estoppel because he, the defendant, "not only failed to invoke the doctrine of estoppel before the learned Subordinate Judge but joined issue with the plaintiff upon the question whether the defendant was not a North-Indian Brahmin and accordingly an issue was raised and evidence adduced on this question."
The court upheld the finding of fact that the appellant, Rajendra Ram Doss, was not a North-Indian Brahmin, and was therefore not qualified to be the mohunt under the established custom.

The appellant's argument to treat the previous mohunt's tenure as an 'interregnum' and revert to the prior line of succession fails because it would lead to the "whole line of succession will be broken beyond repair or redemption, for, once it is accepted that Rajendra Ram Doss is not a· North-Indian Brahmin there is no other Jiving disciple of Narayan Doss who could restore the original line of succession."
why_respondent_won: The appellant, by joining issue on the factual question of his Brahmin status at trial, put the matter at large, allowing the respondent to prove that the appellant was not a North-Indian Brahmin, thereby defeating the estoppel claim.

The High Court made a clear finding of fact, which this Court saw no reason to discard, that the respondent, Devendra Doss, "is a North-Indian Brahmin and is therefore fit to hold the office of a mohunt according to the custom of this Mutt."
The respondent is entitled to succeed as he was the "senior-most disciple of Chetan Doss who had been the reigning mohunt upto the point of time when the dispute regarding succession arose."

Appointing the respondent is the "only possible way in which the old custom may be re-established is by making a fresh start from the point of the death of Chetan Doss and that can only be done by allowing Devendra Doss to be the Mohunt."
policy_considerations: It is not open to the Court to lay down a new rule of succession or to alter the rule of succession completely.

The only way to save the custom is by accepting something as a fact which has so far been accepted by everybody concerned with the Mutt as a fact and which cannot any longer be undone without demolishing altogether the custom of the Mutt.
